changedBeliefs: Invalidation-grouped rerun batching does NOT help reactive fan-out, and specifically regresses the metric that matters. Under table/column-level invalidation one write dirties every stream projecting the changed column (100 in `high_cardinality_fanout`), so batching those reruns into one message per worker is a natural-looking amortization. It was implemented internally (SelectIfChangedBatchRequest + worker loop, ReaderPool.selectBatchIfChanged, batched StreamEngine._flushQueue/_requeryBatch, lastRowCount cost-gate) with no public API change. Clean cross-worktree A/B (two binaries, 3 alternated rounds, warm regime) measured single-write emission latency SLOWER on every lane: homogeneous +22% p50 / +59% p95, heterogeneous +66% p50 / +52% p95. The mechanism: a batched reply is indivisible, so the one changed stream's fresh result is delivered only when its whole batch finishes — it waits behind ~24 cheap unchanged batch-mates' re-hashes. Message-count amortization is the wrong lever for a latency-bound workload. This is the third rejection of the same trade (exp 148 reduced completion callbacks but regressed measured elapsed; exp 239 rejected shared indivisible replies). The lastRowCount cost-gate keeps a large partition off the critical path but not the common many-small-partitions wait.

Methodology, load-bearing: an in-process A/B toggle that flips a hot-path branch inside one warm, long-lived process manufactured a FALSE reproduced win. It reported homogeneous emit latency -25.8% / -27.9% and `ab_drift_check.dart` classified it REPRODUCED across an order flip — yet a clean two-binary cross-worktree comparison of the same code showed a +22% to +66% regression. Order-flipping controls for cross-phase ordering but not for the shared warm JIT/inline-cache/isolate/reader-pool state both arms ride on, nor for a drain probe that keeps the main isolate spinning. For dispatch/scheduling/isolate-message changes, trust only cross-worktree (or the tracelite two-root wrapper); a single-process toggle delta is suspect regardless of what the drift classifier says.

The stream fan-out latency workload was previously unmeasured end-to-end for the suppressed-rerun case. `high_cardinality_fanout`'s settle returns after a fixed 200 ms quiet window keyed on emission counts, so when 99 of 100 reruns suppress their emission (the dominant case) it never waits for those reruns to drain — its 'write burst' number is write dispatch + a constant, not rerun-processing cost. `stream_rerun_latency.dart` (single-write, per-emit completer) is the lane that actually exposes fan-out emission latency, and it is what made this rejection visible.
nextSignals: Do not retry invalidation-grouped rerun batching as a latency play. The batched reply is indivisible, so any grouping delays the one result a subscriber waits on behind its batch-mates — reproduced against a clean baseline here. Reopen ONLY for a throughput-bound stream workload (sustained multi-write backlog where total rerun drain dominates and per-emission latency is provably not the binding constraint, e.g. batch materialized-view refresh, not interactive list views), AND only with a design that preserves independent completion — e.g. the worker streaming each member's result back as it finishes — which removes most of the message-amortization the idea rested on.

Reuse the cross-worktree A/B for any stream-dispatch or reader-message change; do not accept a single-process toggle delta. `stream_rerun_latency.dart` is the durable single-write fan-out emission-latency gate (homogeneous small partitions + heterogeneous large/small); run it on baseline and candidate worktrees. It caught a regression that an emission-count or total-drain summary would have hidden.

The reader pool is 4 workers and each worker's connection steps one query at a time, so a 100-stream fan-out already serializes into ~25 waves regardless of message shape — the reruns are latency-bound on the serial connection, not on the pool. Message-passing overhead (exp 136's ~18 us/call) is real but is not the binding cost for emission latency; removing it does not help the changed stream get its result sooner.
